content: Ovarian follicles are the fundamental units of female reproductive biology. These structures are roughly spherical clusters of cells located within the ovary. Each ovarian follicle contains a single oocyte, also known as an ovum or egg. Periodically, these follicles are stimulated to grow and develop, ultimately leading to the ovulation of a single mature and competent oocyte. Structure The ovarian follicle is composed of several types of cells, including the oocyte, granulosa cells, and the cells of the internal and external theca layers. Oocyte The oocyte within a follicle is in the stage of a primary oocyte. The nucleus of this primary oocyte is referred to as the germinal vesicle. Granulosa Cells The oocyte is surrounded by a glycoprotein layer called the zona pellucida (or zona striata). This layer is further enveloped by granulosa cells. In early tertiary follicles, the granulosa cells that connect the oocyte to the rest of the granulosa cells form a structure known as the cumulus oophorus or discus proligerus. Theca Layers The granulosa cells are enclosed by a thin layer of extracellular matrix called the follicular basement membrane or basal lamina. Beyond this basal lamina, the theca interna and theca externa layers are found. Development Primordial follicles are microscopic and cannot be seen with the naked eye. These follicles progress through stages of development, becoming primary, secondary, and eventually mature vesicular follicles. Mature vesicular follicles are sometimes referred to as Graafian follicles, named after Regnier de Graaf. In humans, oocytes are formed in the ovary before birth and can remain dormant for up to 50 years before being activated. After ovulation, the ruptured follicle transforms into a structure called the corpus luteum. Development of Oocytes in Ovarian Follicles The entire process of folliculogenesis, from primordial to preovulatory follicles, occurs during the first stage of meiosis in oogenesis. During embryonic development, the process does not differ significantly from that of males and follows a shared pathway until gametogenesis. However, once gametogonia enter the gonadal ridge, they begin to associate with somatic cells. As development continues, gametogonia differentiate into oogonia, which become fully surrounded by a layer of pre-granulosa cells. Oogonia proliferate through mitotic division, but this proliferation ceases when the oogonia enter meiosis. The duration of mitotic proliferation is species-specific. In humans, mitotic division of oogonia occurs until the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Once the meiotic process begins, the oogonia, now referred to as primary oocytes, can no longer replicate. Consequently, the total number of gametes is established at this stage. After primary oocytes cease dividing, they enter a prolonged resting phase known as the dictyate stage. This resting phase can last up to 50 years in humans. For each primary oocyte that undergoes meiosis, only one functional oocyte is produced. The other two or three cells formed during this process are called polar bodies, which have no functional role and eventually degenerate. The primary oocyte develops into a secondary oocyte within mature ovarian follicles. Unlike sperm, the egg remains arrested in the secondary stage of meiosis until fertilization occurs. Upon fertilization by a sperm cell, the secondary oocyte completes the second part of meiosis and becomes a zygote. Pathology Any ovarian follicle that grows larger than approximately two centimeters in diameter is classified as an ovarian cyst.
